A. Packing for a day out and printing a class poster

Packing for a day out can be easier when you think through the actual journey rather than collect everything you might possibly want. A useful bag supports the plan without becoming a burden.

Begin with the essential requirements. Tickets, agreed supplies and any instructions from the organiser should come before extra entertainment. ____1____ This prevents a full bag from hiding the one item you truly need.

Check how long you will carry the bag. A comfortable load at home may feel different after a long walk. ____2____ The journey matters as much as the destination.

Put things where you can reach them when needed. A ticket buried beneath lunch creates unnecessary searching at the entrance. ____3____ Small decisions about order can save repeated unpacking.

Keep appropriate items separate. A wet coat and dry paper should not share the same unprotected space. ____4____ Follow any specific storage guidance for food or equipment.

Finally, review the bag once it is packed. ____5____ Removing an unnecessary item can be more useful than finding another pocket. The aim is to carry what the day requires while leaving enough attention and energy to enjoy it.

B. Packing for a day out and printing a class poster

Our class designed a poster for a reading afternoon. The teacher ____1____ (bring) a sample print so we could compare the page on a screen with one on paper. The two did not look exactly alike.

Several ____2____ (design) used a dark background. It made the title dramatic as well ____3____ easy to notice, but some small words became difficult to read. We needed to check the details, not only admire the first impression.

I looked at ____4____ (I) draft from the back of the room. A pale line had almost disappeared. The teacher asked me ____5____ (change) its colour before making another sample.

There was room ____6____ a short date line beneath the title. We made sure the date and place were not separated by a decorative picture. Someone looking quickly should be able to find both.

The second version was ____7____ (clear) than the first. We checked the spelling ____8____ (careful), comparing the words with the approved event details. Each poster ____9____ (check) before it was put on a noticeboard.

The finished design still used colour and pictures, but its practical information no longer depended on a viewer coming very close. We had tested it in a place like the one where people would see it. That was ____10____ useful step between making an attractive page and making a message that worked for its readers.

A. Watching a short film and labelling a model

Watching a short film closely can involve more than following its plot. Images, sounds and the order of scenes influence how the story is experienced. A manageable second viewing can help you notice those choices.

originalGroup.material:
A. Comparing source accounts and describing an old letter

When two accounts describe the same event differently, choosing the more confident voice is not enough. A useful comparison examines how each account came to be written and what it can reasonably establish.

Identify the writer's position in relation to the event. Was the person present, repeating another account or writing much later? ____1____ Nearness can matter without guaranteeing accuracy.

Check what the account was intended to do. A private note and a public speech may select details for different reasons. ____2____ Purpose is part of context, not an automatic reason to dismiss a source.

Distinguish a factual conflict from a difference of emphasis. Two writers can choose different details without making incompatible claims. ____3____ That keeps the comparison from inventing a disagreement.

Look for independent information that addresses the particular uncertainty. ____4____ More copies of one original account do not necessarily provide more independent support.

State what remains unresolved. ____5____ A responsible conclusion can explain why one point is well supported while another remains open. Comparing sources is not a promise that every conflict will end with a single complete story.

B. Comparing source accounts and describing an old letter

In a fictional archive workshop, our class examined a reproduced letter. The tutor ____1____ (explain) that the date on the page and the date of a later copy needed to be recorded separately.

A. Choosing a shared book and making name cards

Choosing a book for shared reading involves more than finding one person who loves it. The group needs a workable way to encounter and discuss the same text.

Begin with practical access. Check whether everyone can obtain a suitable copy in time. ____1____ A popular choice is not useful if half the group cannot read it.

Agree a manageable section for the first meeting. ____2____ A modest beginning can help the group discover its pace before making a longer commitment.

Leave room for different responses. One reader may notice humour while another finds the same scene uncomfortable. ____3____ Ask what in the text led to each response.

Avoid turning the meeting into a memory test. People may bring notes or revisit a passage while speaking. ____4____ Shared attention matters more than proving who recalls the most details.

At the end, check how the arrangement worked. ____5____ The next choice can respond to that experience. A reading group can be thoughtful without making every meeting difficult to prepare for, and friendly without requiring everyone to admire the same book.

B. Choosing a shared book and making name cards

Our class made name cards for a welcome afternoon. The teacher ____1____ (bring) the approved visitor list and asked us to check it before writing on the final paper.

Several ____2____ (name) were unfamiliar to us. We checked their spelling as well ____3____ the order of the words. Guessing from a familiar-looking name could create a mistake.

I looked at ____4____ (I) first card and noticed that the letters were too close together. The teacher asked me ____5____ (leave) more space before trying again. The card would be seen from across a table.

There was room ____6____ a short role description below each name. We used only the wording the visitors had agreed to provide. The card did not need unrelated personal information.

The second version was ____7____ (clear) than the first. We copied the remaining names ____8____ (careful), checking one card at a time. Each card ____9____ (check) against the list before it was placed in its stand.

During the afternoon, the cards helped pupils find the person they wanted to speak with. One visitor asked for a small correction, and we made it promptly without drawing attention to the error. Afterwards, we kept the reusable stands and followed the teacher's arrangement for the printed cards. It was ____10____ useful lesson in making a small public detail accurate, readable and respectful.

A. Giving useful feedback and testing a diagram

Feedback on a draft can help its writer make decisions, but only if the comments are specific enough to use. A page covered in praise or criticism may still leave the next step unclear.

Begin by identifying the draft's intended purpose. A short invitation and an explanatory essay need different things. ____1____ Otherwise you may recommend changes that improve the wrong task.

Describe a particular reading experience. ____2____ A writer can examine a named transition more easily than a general complaint that the whole piece is confusing.

Distinguish a clear error from a preference. A wrong date needs correction; a sentence you would phrase differently may already work. ____3____ That helps the writer weigh the importance of each comment.

Explain the reason behind a suggested change. ____4____ The writer may find another solution that achieves the same aim more naturally.

Finally, leave the writer room to decide. ____5____ Useful feedback supports revision without pretending there is only one acceptable version. A respectful exchange can be direct about a problem while recognising that the work still belongs to its author.

B. Giving useful feedback and testing a diagram

Our group prepared a diagram showing how books moved through a class exchange. The teacher ____1____ (ask) us to include returns as well as the first borrowing step, because the process did not end when a book left the shelf.

Several ____2____ (arrow) connected the boxes. We wanted to show the sequence as well ____3____ the choices available at each point. One arrow went straight to the end, leaving out the return check.

I showed ____4____ (we) first version to another group. They could not tell what happened when a book was damaged. The teacher encouraged us ____5____ (add) the agreed contact step rather than invent a new rule ourselves.

There was room ____6____ a small note explaining which parts depended on teacher approval. We placed it beside the relevant branch, not far away below the whole picture.

The revised diagram was ____7____ (easy) to follow than before. A new reader checked it ____8____ (independent), tracing one possible journey through the boxes. Each missing connection ____9____ (mark) for correction.

The final version did not replace the class rules. It helped people see their order and find where to ask for help. We tested both an ordinary return and one case needing attention. A neat diagram could still hide a broken path, so following the arrows was more useful than admiring the layout. It was ____10____ important step in checking whether a visual explanation actually explained the process.

originalGroup.material:
A. Checking a definition and revising a caption

An argument can become difficult to assess when a key term changes meaning along the way. Checking definitions is therefore part of following the reasoning, not merely a preliminary vocabulary exercise.

Identify the term doing important work. Notice how it is used in the claim and in the evidence offered for that claim. ____1____ Familiar words can carry different senses in different contexts.

Ask whether the writer supplies a definition or relies on ordinary usage. ____2____ Either approach may work, but the reader needs enough consistency to follow the argument.

Watch for a shift between a narrow and a broad meaning. ____3____ Evidence about one specific measure may not establish a claim about the larger concept.

If you question the term, propose the relevant distinction rather than merely calling it vague. ____4____ A concrete alternative helps show where the reasoning needs clarification.

Finally, reread the conclusion with the clarified meaning in mind. ____5____ A definition is useful when it helps determine what has actually been established. It should not become an impressive opening statement that the rest of the argument quietly ignores.

B. Checking a definition and revising a caption

In a fictional town exhibition, our class revised a caption for a photograph of a public celebration. The coordinator ____1____ (explain) that the image showed one moment, not every person's experience of the event.

Several ____2____ (source) described the day. We noted the photographer as well ____3____ the person who later donated the print. Those roles should not be merged simply because both names appeared in the catalogue.

I checked ____4____ (I) first caption. It claimed that everyone in the town had welcomed the event. The coordinator asked me ____5____ (identify) the evidence for that word everyone. A smiling group in one photograph could not establish universal agreement.

There was room ____6____ a short statement describing what was actually visible. We named the location and the group when the records supported them, while removing a claim the image could not carry.

The revised caption was ____7____ (precise) than the first. Another pupil read it ____8____ (critical), checking whether each statement was observation or interpretation. Each final caption ____9____ (approve) before the display was printed.

The work did not require making every sentence hesitant. It required matching confidence to the source. A clear statement about a particular visible group was more informative than a sweeping claim about the whole town. That was ____10____ useful lesson in allowing a photograph to remain valuable without asking it to prove more than it showed.
